newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish economy overstretched in some respects - C.Bank.
newsitem.headline: Irish economy overstretched in some respects - C.Bank.

text.p: Ireland's central bank said on Thursday that it believes the economy is now overstretched in certain respects and that evidence of sectoral bottlenecks is beginning to emerge.
In its quarterly bulletin, the bank said there had been a resurgence of consumption spending in the past year and domestic demand rather than net exports was now the principal factor driving growth.

Buoyant employment prospects, increasing real disposable income and the effects of substantial increases in the value of housing and stock market wealth were likely to contribute to a continuation of strong consumer demand.
"A deceleration in consumer demand is desirable in order to ensure solid sustainable growth in the economy rather than a boom followed by an abrupt downward adjustment further ahead," the bank said.
The bank said that in view of the already strong demand, Ireland's budget strategy was too expansionary.
It noted that in the Irish economy monetary policy was not the most effective instrument in influencing demand and said that fiscal policy should assume a greater stabilisation role.
The full annual value of the discretionary measures announced in Ireland's 1997 budget amounted to 650 million Irish pounds or nearly 1.75 percent of GNP.
The bank said the main effects of this were likely to be felt through the boost to personal disposable incomes of 2.5 percent on a full-year equivalent basis.
"This supports a pro-cyclical strategy at a time when the economy is already under threat of overheating," it added.

The central bank said an increase in the household sector's savings ratio in 1997 would be welcome, following a fall last year, in order to avert a possibly damaging surge in spending including a continuing housing boom.
"Recent trends in house prices are disturbing and some correction is desirable," the bank said.
The principal task of macroeconomic policy in the year ahead must be to prevent an unsustainable expansion and the inevitable disruption and adjustment costs that would follow from that, it said.
